module.admin_panels.checks: Probes common admin paths (/admin, /wp-admin, /phpmyadmin, /grafana…) and tells a real discovery from a false positive: catch-all "not found" page, trailing-slash redirect, and 401/403 the server returns for any URL.
module.admin_panels.fix:
Cut public access without waiting: for each flagged path, let in only the team's IP addresses or a VPN, with a rule in the web server (see the snippet), the web application firewall, the host's security group or the CDN.
If the tool is no longer used (phpMyAdmin, Adminer, Tomcat Manager, old back office, test console): uninstall it and delete its files, instead of merely hiding it or renaming its address.
For an administration that is needed: publish it only on the internal network or behind a VPN, or make it listen on `127.0.0.1` and reach it through an SSH tunnel. Failing that, add authentication in front (single sign-on, client certificate or HTTP authentication) on top of the product's own login.
Protect the login: enable two-factor authentication, require unique and long passwords, delete default or unused accounts, and limit attempts (temporary lockout, fail2ban or a web application firewall rule).
Keep the product and its extensions up to date: exposed admin panels are attacked with published flaws.
If the panel was reachable from the Internet, review its logs and the server's for unknown sign-ins, and as a precaution change the administration passwords, keys and tokens.
A 401 or 403 response means the panel exists but asks for authentication: it is still exposed to credential attacks. Restrict it by IP address or VPN anyway.
Check: from an unauthorized network (for example over 4G), `curl -I https://example.com/wp-admin/` must return `403` or fail to connect; then run the scan again.
module.admin_panels.title: Admin panels
module.admin_panels.why: An admin panel reachable from the Internet is a prime target (credential attacks, known product flaws). Restricting it by IP or VPN greatly reduces the attack surface.
